title: Conditionals and Boolean Logic
oneLiner: if, else if and elif, comparison and logical operators, short-circuit evaluation, Python truthiness versus C#'s strict bools, the conditional expression, and switch versus match.
keyTakeaway: && / and and || / or short-circuit: the right side runs only when it can change the answer, which makes "check it isn't null, then use it" safe in one condition. Python treats 0, empty strings, empty collections and None as false; C# accepts only real bools. In Python's match, a bare name in a case captures instead of comparing.
explanation:
A conditional lets a program make a decision: run this code only if something is true, otherwise run that. The thing being tested is a condition, an expression that is either true or false. Values that are only ever true or false are called booleans (bool in both languages), after George Boole, who worked out the algebra of true and false in the 1840s.

Conditions are built from comparisons (is this bigger than that, are these equal) joined with logical operators: and (both must be true), or (at least one must be true) and not (flip it). Both languages stop working out an and/or as soon as the answer is certain, which is called short-circuit evaluation and is used deliberately all the time.

The languages differ on what may appear in a condition. C# insists on a real bool. Python lets any value stand in a condition and decides whether it counts as true (truthy) or false (falsy): zero, empty text, empty collections and None are falsy. That's convenient and idiomatic, and also a source of bugs when 0 or empty text is a valid value.

For choosing among many cases there's C#'s switch (a statement and, more usefully, an expression that produces a value) and Python's match, which arrived in Python 3.10 and does structural pattern matching: it can check the shape of a value and pull pieces out of it, not just compare it with constants.
